item.title: Deepgram Optimizes Nova-3 Speech-to-Text Model Using AWS Trainium2
item.description:
Deepgram Optimizes Nova-3 Speech-to-Text Model Using AWS Trainium2

Deepgram has collaborated with AWS to port its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to AWS Trainium2 to improve inference efficiency for offline batch workloads, such as medical transcription and contact-center analytics.

⚙️ Key details

Deepgram and the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) team transitioned Nova-3 from standard PyTorch code to AWS Trainium2 using the following process:

  • Initial Porting: Used TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch integration of the Neuron Compiler, supporting both eager execution and torch.compile.
  • Compilation: The model was first run in eager mode to identify CPU fallbacks, then compiled with torch.compile as separate static-shape graphs for the encoder and decoder, resulting in no CPU fallbacks.
  • Accuracy Validation: Numerical accuracy was verified via layer-level output consistency against CPU and end-to-end Word Error Rate (WER).
  • Kernel Optimization: Replaced several layers with fused kernels from the public NKI Library (NKILib), including:
    • Fused QKV projections
    • Fused feed-forward network (FFN) layers
    • Depthwise 1D convolution
  • Infrastructure: The final configuration runs eight model replicas on a single Amazon EC2 trn2.3xlarge instance.

💡 Why it matters

Serving efficiency determines the amount of audio Deepgram can process within a specific infrastructure budget. By utilizing AWS AI chips, Deepgram achieved the following:

  • Cost Efficiency: Processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar on offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads compared to previous compute options.
  • Scalability: These gains allow Deepgram to scale more efficiently and provide models to customers at lower prices.
  • Customer Benefit: These improvements extend to customers self-hosting Deepgram models in their own virtual private cloud (VPC) on Amazon SageMaker AI.

🚀 Availability

Deepgram models are available through:

  • The Deepgram API
  • Self-hosted environments, including Amazon SageMaker AI

#Deepgram #AWS #Trainium2 #SpeechToText #InferenceOptimization

Source: How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium | Amazon Web Services

item.title: ReplaySSM Restores Fast Decoding for State‑Space Layers in Hybrid LLMs
item.description:
ReplaySSM Restores Fast Decoding for State‑Space Layers in Hybrid LLMs

🔍 Overview

Hybrid large‑language models interleave state‑space model (SSM) layers with a few attention layers. Recent work – ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State – shows how to make those SSM layers fast again, removing a major latency bottleneck that appears at serving batch sizes.

🧩 How it works

ReplaySSM changes the way an SSM’s internal state is stored during generation:

  • The state is split into a checkpoint (a full copy of the SSM state) and a buffer of recent inputs.
  • Output computation reads only the buffer, while the checkpoint is updated lazily.
  • This separation eliminates three known problems:
    1. State traffic – the full state no longer moves every token.
    2. Rollback for speculative decoding – the buffer can be discarded without reverting a large state.
    3. Error accumulation in a quantized state – rounding errors no longer re‑enter the recurrence each step.

⚙️ Key details

  • Hybrid model examples – NVIDIA Nemotron 3, Qwen 3.5 through 3.8, Kimi‑K3, and GLM‑5.3‑Flash all use this pattern, with Mamba‑2, Gated DeltaNet (GDN), or Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) as the SSM layer.
  • Decoding bottleneck – at batch size 256 on a Blackwell Ultra B300 GPU, SSM layers dominate latency up to 100 K tokens of context (Figure 2, left). The model has five times as many SSM layers as attention layers.
  • State size comparison – one SSM layer’s FP32 state is 4 MiB per sequence, while an FP8 KV entry is 0.5 KiB per token. Thus an SSM state equals an attention KV cache for roughly 8 K tokens.
  • Speculative decoding – a drafter proposes T tokens, the target model verifies them, then rolls back to the last accepted token. Attention rolls back by moving a KV pointer; an SSM’s state has no cheap inverse, so engines store a full snapshot after each draft token. This costs one read and T writes per step and limits how many requests fit in GPU memory, making speculative decoding barely helpful for SSMs.
  • Quantization issue – the quantized state is both the output and the next update’s input, so rounding error recurs at every step.

🚀 Availability

  • The paper is on arXiv and the implementation is on GitHub.
  • ReplaySSM is integrated into NVIDIA TensorRT‑LLM, vLLM, and FlashInfer.
  • Production deployments include GLM‑5.3‑Flash and Kimi‑K3.

💡 Why it matters

By turning the SSM state into a cache of recent inputs rather than a constantly moved full tensor, ReplaySSM restores the speed advantages of attention‑only models for hybrid architectures. This enables existing speed‑up techniques—speculative decoding and low‑precision quantization—to be applied to models that heavily rely on SSM layers, broadening the practical utility of state‑space approaches in large‑scale inference.

📊 Model‑SSM mapping

Model SSM layer
NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Mamba‑2
Qwen 3.5 – 3.8 Mamba‑2, GDN, or KDA
Kimi‑K3 KDA
GLM‑5.3‑Flash Mamba‑2 / GDN / KDA

#ReplaySSM #SSM #HybridModels #InferenceOptimization

Source: ReplaySSM: Rethinking State Storage for Faster Hybrid-Model Decoding | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA accelerates generative recommender inference with HSTU and Dynamo-Triton
item.description:
NVIDIA accelerates generative recommender inference with HSTU and Dynamo-Triton

NVIDIA has introduced an optimized production workflow for Hierarchical Sequential Transduction Unit (HSTU) generative recommenders using Dynamo-Triton and PyTorch Ahead-of-Time Inductor (AOTI). This update addresses inference challenges in large-scale personalization systems.

🔍 Overview

Generative recommender (GR) systems model user behavior as sequential prediction problems rather than isolated retrieval/ranking stages. HSTUs process high-cardinality event streams of user interactions, context, and items as tokens. This approach excels with long histories and dynamic catalogs but demands low-latency inference despite computational complexity.

🧩 How it works

  • Sequence modeling: User interactions become token sequences for next-item prediction
  • Input composition: Contextual (user), item, and action tokens form categorical inputs
  • Preprocessing: Embeddings are retrieved, interleaved, and positionally encoded
  • HSTU blocks: Process sequences before multitask ranking outputs
  • KV caching: Stores reusable key-value states from prior computations to avoid redundant calculations

⚙️ Key details

Component Function
HSTU Processes sequential token streams for recommendation
PyTorch AOTI Compiles models to optimized artifacts for C++ runtime
FlexKV GPU/host-backed key-value cache for HSTU attention states
NV embedding cache Accelerates high-cardinality embedding lookups

Performance: On RTX PRO 6000 GPUs with 100% KV cache hits:

  • 4.47× speedup (3-layer HSTU) at batch size 8
  • 5.93× speedup (8-layer HSTU) at batch size 8

🚀 Availability

The end-to-end workflow is available through NVIDIA’s recsys-examples repository. Key steps include:

  1. Exporting models via torch.export
  2. AOTI compilation to optimized artifacts
  3. Validation in Python/C++
  4. Deployment via Dynamo-Triton with FlexKV caching

💡 Why it matters

This workflow reduces latency in production GR systems by:

  • Eliminating redundant computations through KV caching
  • Optimizing jagged sequence handling and large embedding tables
  • Enabling efficient serving of long user histories with incremental updates
  • Maintaining sequence modeling benefits while improving throughput

#NVIDIA #AIRecommenders #HSTU #PyTorch #InferenceOptimization

Source: Deploying an HSTU Generative Recommender with NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: DSpark Draft Model for LFM2.5-VL-3B Improves Vision-Language Inference Speed
item.description:
DSpark Draft Model for LFM2.5-VL-3B Improves Vision-Language Inference Speed

An update to the LFM2.5-VL-3B model introduces a DSpark draft model designed to accelerate inference through speculative decoding.

🧩 How it works

The vision drafter uses the same architecture as the text LFM2.5-DSpark drafters. Key technical details include:

  • Architecture: A simplified attention-only drafter with 4 layers and a block size of 9.
  • Mechanism: It captures the target model’s hidden states at a fixed set of tapped layers and conditions on them to draft a block of k candidate tokens.
  • Modality Handling: Image patches and text tokens are projected into a shared representation before the layers, allowing the drafter to operate on hidden-state vectors of identical dimensionality regardless of input modality.
  • Verification: Speculative decoding is exact, as the target verifies every proposed token, ensuring greedy output equals the target alone.

⚙️ Key details

  • Parameter Count: Approximately 280M parameters, increasing the deployed model’s parameter count by 8.9%.
  • Training: The model was trained for 10 epochs on a mixture of vision-language SFT data weighted toward expected workloads.
  • Hardware Recommendation: A block size of 8 or 9 is recommended depending on the hardware.

🚀 Availability

The DSpark draft model is available on Hugging Face in Safetensors and GGUF formats. It ships with day-one support for:

Integration Requirement
llama.cpp Respective build (PR#29339)
MLX-VLM Respective build (PR#2280)
SGLang Build with DSpark support for LFM2 targets (PR #40651)

💡 Why it matters

Speculative decoding accelerates the decode stage of inference, though it does not speed up vision encoding or prefill. Because prefill is compute-bound and grows (sub)quadratically with prompt length, it can occupy a significant portion of end-to-end latency, particularly on edge devices. This follows Amdahl’s law, where overall speedup is capped by the non-accelerated parts of the workload.

Performance measurements across six diverse vision-based tasks (including general VQA, text VQA, image captioning, chart VQA, complex reasoning, and multi-turn conversation) show the following gains using a block size of 8:

  • MLX (M5 Max): Decoding speedups of 2.30x to 3.13x; end-to-end latency improvements of 1.56x to 2.62x.
  • llama.cpp (M3 Ultra): Decoding improvements of 1.57x to 2.14x; end-to-end improvements of 1.30x to 1.77x.
  • H100 GPU: Decoding speedups of 20.4x to 2.66x; end-to-end improvements of 1.64x to 2.27x.

#LFM2.5 #SpeculativeDecoding #VLM #InferenceOptimization

Source: Accelerating vision-language models with LFM2.5-VL-DSpark

item.title: WISE Method Optimizes Recurrent Language Model Inference via Support Exploitation
item.description:
WISE Method Optimizes Recurrent Language Model Inference via Support Exploitation

Researchers have introduced WISE (Working-set Inference with Support Exploitation), a training-free method designed to improve the efficiency of recurrent language models by optimizing how they handle global attention during inference.

🔍 Overview

Recurrent language models refine latent representations by repeatedly applying shared network blocks. However, standard inference typically recomputes global attention at every recurrent step. The developers of WISE discovered that attention support and distributions stabilize substantially earlier than attention outputs and hidden states.

🧩 How it works

WISE leverages the observation that early recurrent steps identify a sparse working set of relevant context, while subsequent steps refine representations using largely the same routing support. The method operates as follows:

  • Early Recurrence: Uses unrestricted global attention.
  • Later Recurrence: Reuses the directly discovered block-structured support.
  • Dynamic Control: Keeps recurrent depth and within-support attention computation dynamic.

⚙️ Key details

Controlled interventions indicated that recurrent discovery is necessary and that support-only reuse preserves model behavior better than more restrictive attention-reuse options. Performance metrics include:

Metric Result
Multi-hop QA Performance Largely preserves full-attention performance
Quality (2K context) Largely preserved
Quality (4K context) Measurable loss
Max Attention Speedup (4K) Up to 1.76x over native FlashAttention
Full 32-step Trajectory Speedup 1.36x

💡 Why it matters

Context scaling reveals that as context increases, working sets become increasingly sparse, leading to greater efficiency gains.

#LLM #InferenceOptimization #AttentionMechanism #RecurrentLanguageModels

Source: Attention Routing Stabilizes Early: Working-Set Inference for Recurrent Language Models
